name: Quichua, dialecto de Cañar
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source.

catalog_quote: Característico del Quichua es que todas sus palabras de más de dos sílabas tengan su mayor fuerza de voz en la penúltima sílaba, es decir un acento grave. Son excepción las preguntas con contracción cuyo acento es agudo. En los siguientes ejemplos se señalan las acentuaciones a través de letras mayúsculas. Ejemplo: ÑUca HUAhua TAita Ahuac MAma comaDROna. El Quichua es una lengua aglutinante, esto es que a una raíz se pueden agregar sufijos, lo cual hace que el acento se modifique, pero el mismo siempre se ubicará en la penúltima sílaba. Así se puede observar, como se ha modificado el acento en los ejemplos anteriores al agregar el sufijo -CA, pero con la característica de que la mayor fuerza de voz se ubica en la penúltima sílaba. Ejemplo: ñuCAca huaHUAca taiTAca aHUACca maMAca comadroNAca.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.translation: It is characteristic of Quichua that all its words of more than two syllables have their greatest force of voice on the penultimate syllable, i.e. a paroxytone accent. The exception is contracted questions, whose accent is oxytone (final). [...] Quichua is an agglutinative language, i.e. suffixes can be added to a root, which causes the accent to move, but it will always be located on the penultimate syllable. [...] Example: ñuCAca, huaHUAca, taiTAca, aHUACca, maMAca, comadroNAca.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is fixed on the penultimate syllable of the word (root plus all suffixes); adding suffixes moves stress rightward so that it stays penultimate. Only contracted (elliptical) questions consisting of a topic plus -ca (e.g. Paicá? 'and he?') are stressed on the final syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: Contracted questions (bare noun/pronoun + -CA used as a question, e.g. PaiCA? 'and he?', CanCA? 'and you?') carry final (agudo) stress (sec.7 p.17: '-CA.. hace las veces de sufijo de pregunta si se acentúa en forma aguda'). Cordero 1892 p.XLV adds a handful of final-stressed items attributed to Spanish-influenced intonation or emphatic lengthening (chugmál, gullán, lulún, ajá, atatáy). Carpenter 1982 pp.183-184 adds paralinguistic focus stress on a root or suffix.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the full agglutinated word including suffixes (examples show stress moving with -ca). Author states questions do not require special intonation. Pedagogical grammar written in and for the Cañar dialect; independent confirmation for Azuay from Cordero 1892 (p.XLV, 'todas graves.. acento prosódico en la penúltima sílaba') and for Cañar/S. Chimborazo/Azuay within Carpenter 1982 p.182 ('non-phonemic; it falls on the penultimate syllable, and shifts to the right when suffixes are added').
new_statements.identity_note: Maldonado Córdova 1995 describes specifically the Quichua of Cañar province (written at the Instituto Quichua of the Misión Luterana Sudamericana de Noruega in the city of Cañar; 'dialecto de Cañar'), the core of cana1262. Cordero 1892 describes Azuay (Cuenca) Quichua, also within cana1262. Carpenter 1982 is a pan-Ecuadorian description whose phonology chapter draws primarily on Imbabura, Cañar, Loja and Napo and explicitly lists South Chimborazo (Sch), Cañar (Cñr) and Azuay (Azy) among the non-central highland dialects.

tone.quote: The different Ecuadorian Quichua languages have anywhere from 23 to 28 consonants, and 3 vowels. Quichua essentially has no suprasegmental* phonemes*: unlike Spanish and English, phonetic* stress or accent is almost entirely predictable, falling in almost all cases on the penultimate (next to last) syllable, and does not need to be written23. [fn. 23:] There is one very small exception to this rule, in which the accent shifts to the final syllable on the last word in the sentence in some cases, but this does not negate the general fact that accent is not phonemic* in Quichua on individual words like it is in Spanish or English.
tone.locator: §4.1 'Phonemes of Ecuadorian Quichua / Fonemas del quichua ecuatoriano', p. 21 of the 2nd edition (23-Oct-2020), with footnote 23 on the same page; restated p. 40: 'Stress in Quichua is non-phonemic*, and always falls on the penultimate syllable.'
tone.summary: No tone: the grammar states Ecuadorian Quichua has essentially no suprasegmental phonemes at all; word stress is non-phonemic, fixed penultimate, with a marginal sentence-final shift to the last syllable (e.g. stressed -cá).
